summary: A white paper describing Simple Internet Protocol Plus (SIPP), one of the candidate designs for the Next Generation of IP. It was submitted to the IPng effort and is informational.

eli5.summary: One team's idea for a bigger, better address system for the internet.

questions: how does sipp address transition from ipv4
subtitle: Design overview of the next generation Internet Protocol with 64-bit addresses

tldr.problem: IPv4 is running out of address space and cannot efficiently support future growth in emerging markets like mobile devices, networked entertainment, and device control. Its header format is also inefficient and lacks built-in security and quality-of-service features.
tldr.mechanism: Simple Internet Protocol Plus (SIPP) expands addresses from 32 to 64 bits, simplifies the header, moves options to separate extension headers, adds flow labeling for quality of service, includes security capabilities, and provides mechanisms for seamless transition from IPv4.
tldr.outcome: SIPP was accepted as the basis for IPv6 (RFC 2460), the standard next-generation Internet Protocol. It enables the Internet to scale to billions of devices with built-in support for mobility, auto-configuration, and security.

today: SIPP was accepted as the basis for IPv6 and standardized in RFC 2460. IPv6 has been deployed globally for over two decades, particularly in Asia and among major content providers, and remains the standard next-generation Internet Protocol.

sections.title: Overview of SIPP
sections.content:
Simple Internet Protocol Plus (SIPP) is a new version of IP designed as an evolutionary successor to IPv4. Rather than making radical changes, SIPP retained IPv4 functions that work and removed or improved those that do not. SIPP was assigned IP version number 6. The protocol is designed to be simple enough that a developer familiar with IPv4 could implement a basic SIPP system from the specification alone.

The white paper explains SIPP in four main parts: the problem it solves (scaling and new market requirements), the key design decisions, why SIPP is the right solution, and transition mechanisms that allow IPv4 and SIPP to coexist. The document was submitted to the IETF's IPng (Internet Protocol Next Generation) working group as one of the candidate proposals for the next standard Internet Protocol.

SIPP was designed to work well on high-performance networks like ATM while remaining efficient for low-bandwidth networks like wireless. It can be installed as a normal software upgrade with no coordination required (no "flag days"), and SIPP hosts can interoperate with IPv4 hosts indefinitely as long as IPv4 addresses remain globally unique.
sections.eli5: SIPP is a new version of IP (the protocol that routes data across the Internet) that has bigger addresses to support more devices, a cleaner design, and security built in from the start.

sections.title: Key Issues for IPng
sections.content:
The primary driver for a next-generation IP is growth. IPv4 was designed when the Internet was small; by 1994, the number of networks in the Internet was doubling approximately every 12 months. IPv4's 32-bit addresses support about 4 billion unique devices, a limit the Internet was approaching. IPv4 addressing and routing are also not hierarchical enough to aggregate efficiently under Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR), straining global routing tables.

Beyond address space, IPng must solve the transition problem. The Internet is too large for controlled rollout. Any new protocol must allow gradual, uncoordinated deployment with IPv4 and IPng hosts coexisting indefinitely. It must be backward compatible in spirit: just as Intel processors remain compatible with earlier generations and operating systems maintain backward compatibility with applications, IPng must not force everyone to upgrade simultaneously.

Emerging markets also drive new requirements. Nomadic personal computing devices with wireless, infrared, and wired network interfaces will become ubiquitous; they need built-in mobility support and authentication. Networked entertainment including television on demand and interactive services requires low overhead and auto-configuration. Device control for lighting, heating, and motors demands simple, robust, cost-effective solutions. All these markets will proceed with or without an IETF standard; if IETF IPng does not serve them, they will develop proprietary protocols.
sections.eli5: IPv4 addresses are running out because so many things need to connect to the Internet. A new protocol must be easy to switch to gradually, support mobile devices, and work for new uses like talking televisions and smart lights.

sections.title: SIPP Header and Addressing
sections.content:
The SIPP header is only 4 bytes longer than IPv4 (40 bytes vs. 20 bytes) despite doubling the address size, because unnecessary fields were removed. The header contains a version field, a 28-bit Flow Label for quality-of-service labeling, payload length, a payload type selector, a hop limit (equivalent to IPv4's TTL), a 64-bit source address, and a 64-bit destination address. Options are no longer in the header but in separate extension headers that follow, so routers only examine them if necessary.

SIPP addresses are 64 bits long and come in three types. Unicast addresses identify single nodes and come in three forms: global hierarchical addresses (assigned by Internet service providers), local-use addresses (for private networks and auto-configuration), and special addresses for IPv4-only hosts during transition. Cluster addresses allow source-selected policies for choosing among multiple service providers. Multicast addresses include a 4-bit scope field to limit multicast propagation range, improving scalability over IPv4's all-or-nothing multicast.

The 64-bit address space supports 2^64 addresses—four billion times more than IPv4. Addresses can be further extended using the routing option, growing to 128, 192, or more bits while keeping routing efficient with 64-bit units. Global unicast addresses use a provider-oriented hierarchy: a compatibility bit, provider ID, subscriber ID, subnet ID, and node ID. This structure supports efficient routing aggregation.
sections.eli5: SIPP has larger 64-bit addresses and a simpler header that moves extra options to separate sections, so routers can handle normal packets faster.

sections.title: Quality of Service, Routing, and Security
sections.content:
The Flow Label field enables applications to request special handling from routers, such as guaranteed bandwidth or low-latency service for real-time communication. A flow is identified by a source address and a non-zero flow ID assigned by the source host. Hosts select flow IDs pseudo-randomly to allow routers to use any bits as a hash key for efficient table lookup. The drop priority subfield lets applications distinguish which of their packets should be dropped first under congestion—useful for video where synchronization packets matter more than screen updates.

SIPP routing uses address sequences similar to IPv4's loose source route option. Hosts must reverse routes in received packets, enabling new capabilities like provider selection (choosing which ISP to use), host mobility (changing location without breaking connections), and auto-readdressing (changing addresses while remaining reachable). The first and last addresses in a sequence identify the connection, while middle addresses can change, allowing transport-layer connections to survive address changes.

SIPP includes integrated security as a core feature. The Authentication Header provides integrity and authentication without confidentiality (using keyed MD5), making it exportable under export restrictions while preventing masquerading attacks. The Encapsulating Security Payload adds confidentiality (using DES CBC). Both are optional but always available, allowing each user to choose their security level. This layered approach ensures security serves all users' needs without forcing unnecessary overhead on those who do not need it.
sections.eli5: SIPP can mark packets to get special treatment like fast delivery for video calls, let senders choose which Internet company to use, support moving to a new network without losing connections, and encrypt data from the start.

sections.title: Transition from IPv4
sections.content:
Successful transition is central to SIPP's design. The mechanism is called IPAE (once an acronym for "IP Address Encapsulation"), and it has five key elements. First, 64-bit SIPP addressing encompasses the existing IPv4 32-bit space. IPv4 hosts need not change addresses; IPv4 hosts upgraded to SIPP keep their IPv4 addresses as the low 32 bits of a 64-bit SIPP address. Second, SIPP-within-IPv4 tunneling encapsulates SIPP packets in IPv4 headers, allowing SIPP traffic to cross IPv4-only networks with automatic tunnel configuration.

Third, dual-stack SIPP hosts can directly interoperate with IPv4 hosts on the same subnet and across the Internet, using algorithms to determine when IPv4 is reachable and when SIPP must be used. Fourth, header translation allows SIPP-only hosts to communicate with IPv4-only hosts and vice versa, bridging the two protocols at the network edge. Fifth, optional IPv4 address-to-SIPP mapping could improve IPv4 routing scalability, though this feature is optional given the success of CIDR.

These mechanisms ensure SIPP and IPv4 can coexist for a decade or more without any "flag day" cutover. Hosts can upgrade at their own pace, network operators can deploy incrementally, and vendors can integrate SIPP into products on their own schedules. This flexibility protects the enormous investment in IPv4 while allowing gradual migration.
sections.eli5: IPv4 and SIPP can run together on the same networks using tunnels and translation, so everything doesn't have to change at once—people can upgrade whenever they want.

sections.title: SIPP Effort and Outcomes
sections.content:
SIPP developed from the merger of three IETF working groups. The original IPAE group focused on addressing and transition mechanisms. Steve Deering's Simple Internet Protocol (SIP) group worked on a simplified header with 64-bit addresses and extension headers. Paul Francis's "P" Internet Protocol (Pip) group contributed advanced features like provider selection and mobility. The groups realized these could be combined; Pip's features could be added to SIP's simpler core using extension headers, while keeping IPAE's transition mechanisms. The merged effort became SIPP, chaired by Steve Deering, Paul Francis, and Robert Hinden.

By the time RFC 1710 was written in October 1994, numerous organizations were actively implementing SIPP and IPAE: Digital Equipment Corp., Sun, Xerox PARC, Naval Research Lab, Network General, and others. Implementations covered multiple operating systems and platforms including Solaris, OSF/1, BSD, Mac OS, DOS/Windows, and Open VMS, with support for core protocols like telnet, FTP, ping, and UDP.

SIPP's broad support and evolutionary design made it the consensus choice for IPng. It was standardized as IPv6 in RFC 2460. The protocol successfully addressed the scaling problem, provided a clear transition path, and laid the foundation for the next generation of Internet services including mobile computing, real-time communication, and ubiquitous connectivity.
sections.eli5: SIPP brought together ideas from three different teams, many companies implemented it, and it became the standard for IPv6, the new version of IP that powers today's Internet.
